turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hi, Doc. Well, I'm here because... I just can't stop seeing this rough, sunken-looking patch on my face. Whenever I look in the mirror, or if I see a photo of myself, it's all I can focus on. It makes one side of me look all old and beat-up. It's really getting to me, even though people keep saying they barely notice anything at all.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes an intense preoccupation with a perceived flaw on their face that is all they can focus on, despite others reporting they barely notice anything.

turns.doctor_question: How much is this concern about your face affecting your daily life? For example, is it interfering with work, school, relationships, or social activities?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's definitely messing with things. I've been running late for work lately—I'm a construction laborer—because I just get stuck looking in the mirror, trying to fix it or hide it before I can get out the door. And on the job, I've started dodging the site photos they take sometimes. I just... I don't want any pictures of my face out there. 

It's bleeding into my personal life, too. I've even been skipping out on some of our family game nights. I just can't sit there across the table from everyone, thinking they're staring at my face.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient exhibits preoccupation with a perceived facial flaw, avoiding photos and skipping family gatherings out of concern that people are staring at their face.
symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient engages in repetitive appearance-related behaviors, specifically getting stuck checking the mirror and attempting to fix or camouflage their face.

turns.doctor_question: When you look at this rough, sunken patch on your face, how noticeable would you say it actually is compared to how noticeable it feels to you—do you think most people would see it if you pointed it out, or is it something that's much more obvious to you than it would be to anyone else?
turns.patient_response:
Well, like I was saying when I first came in... to me, it's just glaring. I can't stop seeing it. Every time I look in the mirror or catch a glimpse of a photo, that rough, sunken-looking patch is all I can focus on. It just makes that whole side of my face look old and beat-up. 

But I guess... yeah, it must be way more obvious to me than to anyone else. Because, like I mentioned, people keep telling me they barely notice anything at all. Even if I point right at it, my family or the guys at work say it's no big deal or they don't see what I'm talking about. I just don't understand how they don't see what I'm seeing.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes an intense preoccupation with a perceived facial flaw that they cannot stop focusing on, while acknowledging that others barely notice it or cannot see it at all.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been preoccupied with this rough, sunken patch on your face? When did you first start noticing it and becoming concerned about it?
turns.patient_response: I'm not exactly sure when it started, to be honest. It feels like it's been a while now, but I couldn't give you an exact date or anything. It just sort of... became this thing I couldn't stop looking at.

turns.doctor_question: Besides looking in the mirror, what kinds of things do you find yourself doing because of this concern about your face? For example, do you spend time trying to fix it, cover it up, or check how it looks?
turns.patient_response:
Well, before I head to work, or if I'm supposed to go to my sister's for game night... I know you said besides the mirror, but when I'm standing there, I'm constantly turning my face under all the different lights in the bathroom, just trying to see how bad it looks from different angles. And I find myself rubbing at the spot a lot, like maybe I can just smooth it out or something. 

As for covering it up, I'll usually pull my hat down real low over my face so people can't see that side as well. But honestly, if I'm checking it and I think it just looks too obvious that day... I'll just make up an excuse not to go out at all.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient describes engaging in repetitive behaviors in response to appearance concerns, including checking their face under different lighting and angles in the mirror, rubbing at the perceived flaw, and camouflaging with a hat pulled low.

turns.doctor_question: When your family and coworkers tell you they barely notice anything on your face, do you believe them, or do you think they're just being nice or trying not to hurt your feelings?
turns.patient_response: Honestly, I don't really know. Half the time I think they're just being nice, you know, trying to spare my feelings or just get me to stop talking about it. But then... the guys at the site, they aren't exactly the type to tiptoe around somebody's feelings. If something looks messed up, they usually say it. So maybe they really don't see it. I'm just not sure what to believe anymore, because when I look in the mirror, it's just so obvious to me.

turns.doctor_question: When you really think about it, do you believe that the patch on your face is actually as noticeable and severe as it feels to you, or could it be that your mind is making it seem worse than it actually is?
turns.patient_response:
I... man, I really don't know. When I'm just sitting here talking to you about it, I can kind of see how maybe my mind is making a mountain out of a molehill. But then... I go look in the mirror again, and it's just right there. It looks so bad to me. 

So I guess I don't have a straight answer for you. I just don't know if it's actually that severe, or if I'm just driving myself crazy over it.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about the fact that multiple people—your family, your coworkers, even the guys at the construction site—all say they don't see what you're seeing, does that make you question whether there really is something wrong with your face, or are you pretty convinced that it's there no matter what they say?
turns.patient_response:
Honestly, it's pretty much what I was just saying. It does make me question it... sometimes. When the guys at the site and my family all say the exact same thing, it makes me think, alright, maybe it really isn't there, or at least not as bad as I think it is. 

But am I completely convinced that it's all in my head? No. Because I still see it plain as day when I look in the mirror. So... I don't know. I guess I'm just stuck in the middle. I can't really give you a straight yes or no on that, because I'm just not sure myself.

turns.doctor_question: If you were to go to the mirror right now and really look carefully, do you think there's any chance that the patch might not actually be there, or is it absolutely certain that you can see it?
turns.patient_response: If I went and looked in the mirror right now... I'm absolutely certain I'd see it. There's no chance I wouldn't. Every single time I look, it's there. That's the part that messes with me, you know? Even when I start to think maybe everyone else is right and it's not a big deal, the second I look in the mirror, it's just... right there. I see it clear as day.

turns.doctor_question: When you really think about the possibility that the patch might not be there, or might be much less noticeable than you perceive it—does that possibility feel like it could actually be true, or does it feel impossible no matter how hard you try to consider it?
turns.patient_response:
I mean... it doesn't feel completely impossible. Like, sitting here right now, I can see how it might be true that I'm making it worse than it is, especially with what everyone else says. 

But... I don't know. It's hard. When I really try to hold onto that idea, it just doesn't stick. My brain just goes right back to what I see on my face. So I guess I can consider the possibility, but actually believing it deep down? That feels pretty close to impossible.

turns.doctor_question: When you look in the mirror and see that patch on your face, and you think about what everyone else is telling you—that they don't see it—on a scale where 0% means 'I'm 100% sure everyone is right and it's not really there' and 100% means 'I'm 100% sure it's there no matter what anyone says'—where would you place yourself right now?
turns.patient_response:
I'd probably say... maybe somewhere around 70 percent. It's tough to put an exact number on it, but... yeah, around 70. 

I hear what my family and the guys at work are saying, and that keeps me from being at a full 100 percent. I know they don't see it. But because I still see it myself every single time I look, it's definitely past the halfway mark. So, yeah, I guess 70 percent makes the most sense right now.
